question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.
essay:
Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units, but it should do so by strengthening protection inside tenancies rather than by capping initial rents. This position protects tenants without the supply loss that harder caps seem to cause.

Subdivided units are a last resort for many people. About 110,000 households live in them, and tenants pay a 15 to 25 percent premium per square foot compared with mainstream flats [D1p1]. They are mostly new arrivals, single parents and families waiting for public housing, which has averaged about five and a half years [D1p2]. The burden is also getting worse: rent to income rose from 31 to 34 percent for SDU households even after the 2021 ordinance [D2p2]. That is why doing nothing is hard to defend.

But the instrument matters enormously. The evidence against a hard initial-rent cap is strong and comes from three independent directions. First, the academic literature distinguishes first-generation controls (caps on levels), which show "consistent contraction effects," from second-generation controls (caps on increases), which show "small or null effects" [D6p2]. Hong Kong's stable SDU stock, growing from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 [D2p1], is evidence that moderate regulation did not trigger exit, not that a binding cap would be equally harmless. The think-tank debate in the news digest captures exactly this ambiguity: one side reads stable stock as proof that "capacity exists for more control," the other as an artifact of a non-binding instrument [D12p2]. The second reading is more consistent with D6's elasticity estimate of 0.31 to 0.48, which implies a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1]. Modelled for Hong Kong, a 15 percent initial-rent cut delivers about $900/month to incumbents while pricing out 3,000 to 4,000 households per year, "mostly new arrivals and newly formed households" [D6p4]. That is the same population the cap is meant to protect.

Second, the comparative cases reinforce the point. Berlin's Mietendeckel produced a measurable supply contraction within a year as owners withheld or rerouted flats [D7p1], and when the law fell, suppressed increases released into the market and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend line [D7p2]. The Berlin lesson is explicit: "the tenants the cap protects are those already inside, and the bill is handed to those still outside" [D7p3]. New York's second-generation scheme, by contrast, shows only modest contraction because it is "light at first-rent", the exact point Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance also left untouched [D8p2].

Third, enforcement reality undermines the hard-cap case even on its own terms. Inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1]. More damning: the tenants least able to complain, those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], or the newest arrivals, are precisely those a complaint-driven enforcement regime would miss [D10p2]. The subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which "the newest-arrival tail... is protected first rather than last" [D10p3].

The main danger of tightening is that owners leave. The Landlords Association argues that a hard cap on initial rents is confiscatory and says members will convert units back or empty them if returns fall below mortgage cost [D5p1, D5p2]. I take this seriously, but the evidence behind it is thin. The Association admits it has no data on its members' actual margins, and its cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate [D5p3]. A threat is not data.

So what should be done? The NGO report's survey of 440 households found that 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1]. Mr Chan, asked what would help most, "does not name rent. He names the waiting list" [D3p3]. This is not sentimentality; it is revealed preference from the people the policy targets. A narrow tightening, tenure security plus a light indexed band on initial rents, as counsel suggests, defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation [D9p2], addresses the actual pain point without triggering the contraction arithmetic of D6. It also avoids the judicial-review risk that a hard cap framed as deprivation of income stream would almost certainly attract [D9p1].

There are limits to my argument. The post-2023 rent figures rely on survey extrapolation because reporting is voluntary [D2p3], so the recent trend is uncertain. I also cannot prove that a stronger in-tenancy rule would reduce the burden, since the current one did not stop it rising [D2p2]. Still, the evidence supports moving carefully, and it does not support a hard cap.

drafts.text:
Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units, but it should do so by strengthening protection inside tenancies rather than by capping initial rents. This position protects tenants without the supply loss that harder caps seem to cause.

Subdivided units are a last resort for many people. About 110,000 households live in them, and tenants pay a 15 to 25 percent premium per square foot compared with mainstream flats [D1p1]. They are mostly new arrivals, single parents and families waiting for public housing, which has averaged about five and a half years [D1p2]. For these households the unit is not a choice. The burden is also getting worse: rent to income rose from 31 to 34 percent for SDU households [D2p2]. That is why doing nothing is hard to defend.

The current law is limited. The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped rent increases within an existing tenancy but did not cap the starting rent, and it excluded co-living units from key provisions [D1p3]. It did slow things down. SDU rent per square foot grew 6.8 percent in 2019 to 2021 but only 3.1 percent in 2021 to 2023, although private rents overall grew 1.7 percent in that later window [D2p2]. So the ordinance helped, but not enough, because the starting rent was left free.

The main danger of tightening is that owners leave. The Landlords Association argues that a hard cap on initial rents is confiscatory and says members will convert units back or empty them if returns fall below mortgage cost [D5p1, D5p2]. I take this seriously, but the evidence behind it is thin. The Association admits it has no data on its members' actual margins, and its cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate [D5p3]. A threat is not data.

Better evidence comes from research and from Berlin. The working paper separates first-generation controls, which are hard caps on levels, from second-generation controls, which cap increases inside tenancies. Hard caps show consistent contraction, while second-generation controls show small or null effects on stock [D6p2]. Hong Kong's stock kept growing from 107,300 in 2021 to 111,200 in 2025 after the ordinance [D2p1], which fits that pattern. Berlin shows what the other path looks like. After its 2020 cap, listing supply fell within a year as owners withheld flats, and when the law was struck down rents for new contracts jumped above the earlier trend [D7p1, D7p2]. The lesson is that caps protect those already inside and hand the bill to those outside [D7p3].

This is why I do not support a hard cap. The same paper warns that the households who lose units are the same people the cap is meant to protect [D6p3]. If a cap removes 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years for every 10 percent rent cut, as the estimates suggest [D6p1], then new arrivals and families in the queue would pay for it.

My proposal is therefore to tighten the second-generation tools. Extend in-tenancy protection to the co-living units that were excluded [D1p3], and give tenants more security so they can stay in regulated tenancies longer. The working paper says tenant gains depend on how many stay long enough to offset those who cannot find units [D6p3]. This addresses the rising burden without copying Berlin.

There are limits to my argument. The post-2023 rent figures rely on survey extrapolation because reporting is voluntary [D2p3], so the recent trend is uncertain. I also cannot prove that a stronger in-tenancy rule would reduce the burden, since the current one did not stop it rising [D2p2]. Still, the evidence supports moving carefully, and it does not support a hard cap.
